query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Nanocrystalline grain refinement increases the density of microstructural interfaces, which broadens the first‐order magnetostructural transition and reduces hysteretic losses during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles in FeMnNiGeSi alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high-entropy alloys with an ordered single-phase hexagonal structure exhibiting a sharp, hysteretic first-order magnetostructural transition.
generation.intervention: Systematically tune the deposition parameters (for example, reduce substrate temperature and/or increase deposition rate) to achieve grain sizes below ~100 nm, thereby enhancing the density of grain boundaries and nanoscale interfaces.
generation.conditions: Low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles near the as-deposited transition temperatures, ensuring that the modifications remain within the regime where mechanical stability, rare-earth avoidance, and cost-effectiveness are maintained.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased density and uniform distribution of grain boundaries and nanoscale phase interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The refined grain structure introduces a broad distribution of local transition temperatures and transformation kinetics, which spatially distributes the magnetostructural transition. This causes a smoother change in magnetic entropy with temperature, leading to a broadened transition, reduced peak entropy change, lower hysteresis, and enhanced effective heat exchange due to increased surface area.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-deposited baseline, samples with refined nanocrystalline grain sizes will exhibit a broader magnetostructural transition with a lower peak entropy change, reduced hysteresis in low-field cycles, and improved effective heat-exchange rates.
generation.baseline: Bulk forms (arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons) with a coarse-grained, ordered single-phase hexagonal state that display a sharp, high-magnitude but hysteretic entropy change.
generation.boundary: These effects are expected to hold for samples where the average grain size is below approximately 100 nm and the processing does not compromise the alloy's mechanical integrity. The hypothesis may not hold if grain sizes exceed this threshold or if unexpected processing defects emerge.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative mechanism is supported by prior observations linking microstructural integrity to transition kinetics, the quantitative impact on entropy change magnitude and hysteresis reduction remains uncertain without detailed experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeMnNiGeSi samples: one set employing conventional deposition conditions (baseline) and another using controlled deposition parameters aimed at producing grain sizes below ~100 nm. Subject both sets to identical low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
measurements: Grain size distribution via TEM and XRD analysis (peak broadening)
Magnetic entropy change versus temperature profiles
Hysteresis loop measurements during magnetic-cooling cycles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanocrystalline samples do not display a broader magnetostructural transition, reduced peak entropy change, lower hysteresis, and improved heat-exchange rates compared to the as-deposited baseline, then the proposed mechanism—that increased interface density governs the kinetics and reversibility of the transition—will be falsified.

As shown in Fig. 7 for x = 0.12% and x = 2.91%, the curves do not collapse onto a single curve. It is apparent by visual inspection, though, that the degree of collapse increases when Pd is added. We can quantify the degree of collapse using statistical methods, namely the Brown-Forsythe analysis of variance (BF method). The BF method gives a single statistic, F, which directly measures the homogeneity of variance between a group of peaked curves. F is zero when a group of curves is identical, and increases from there as the set of curves becomes more inhomogeneous. This therefore gives us direct evidence that distributions of exchange interactions exist in the material: a small distribution will be essentially a perfect homogeneous material, and will have F approaching zero; a broad distribution will lead to increased F. We observe a decrease in F of at least 50% with annealing or Pd incorporation, and an additional 50% decrease with both annealing and adding Pd content. frame.system: As‐deposited, non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high-entropy alloys that, in their initial state, exhibit an ordered single‐phase hexagonal structure which undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition.
frame.goal: To explain and ultimately control the magnetocaloric response and associated hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles for magnetic refrigeration applications.
frame.limitation: The as-deposited bulk forms (arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons) display a sharp, large but hysteretic entropy change coupled with limited heat-exchange rates (attributable to low surface-to-volume ratios) and prior work has focused only on composition-driven shifts in transition temperature or amplitude, neglecting multi-variable optimization.
root_cause_cues: large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change
frame.regime: Low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles, with conditions bounded by the nominal as-deposited transition temperatures and microstructural scales of the samples.
prior_attempts: Arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons have been used to study the magnetocaloric effect, but these approaches yielded a single-phase hexagonal state with a first-order transition that is highly hysteretic and limited in heat exchange rate due to low surface-to-volume ratio.

Previous efforts concentrated on varying composition as a single optimization variable, which, while shifting transition temperatures or response amplitudes, did not address the sharpness of the transition or the hysteretic losses.
frame.understanding: The hypothesis to test is that the density and distribution of microstructural interfaces (such as grain boundaries or nanoscale phase inhomogeneities), which can be systematically controlled during deposition (for instance, via tuning the deposition rate or substrate temperature to generate a nanocrystalline morphology), are the governing factors that modulate the kinetics and reversibility of the magnetostructural transition. Under this view, a controlled intervention to intentionally reduce the grain size (thus increasing the interface density) should promote a more gradual, spatially distributed transformation. Predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline include a broadened transition (i.e., a less abrupt, lower peak in the entropy-change curve), reduced hysteresis in the low-field regime, and improved effective heat-exchange rates due to the increased surface area. These predictions should hold over a window where the grain size remains in the nanocrystalline domain (e.g., below ~100 nm) and the mechanical stability is preserved. Prior observations supporting this hypothesis include the fact that rapid solidification (e.g., in melt-spun microribbons) already hints at the importance of microstructure on transition sharpness and hysteresis. Conversely, if controlled grain refinement does not lead to a reduction in hysteretic losses or fails to tailor the transition profile as predicted, then this would falsify the proposed mechanism.

decision.trend: Early studies on rare‐earth‐free, transition‐metal based high-entropy alloys for magnetocaloric applications focused on optimizing composition in bulk arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons. Researchers initially targeted shifts in the transition temperature and magnitude of the entropy change. Subsequent work began to recognize that processing methods—notably the rapid solidification in melt-spun forms—alter the density and distribution of microstructural interfaces (e.g., grain boundaries, dislocation networks) that in turn modulate the transformation kinetics and hysteresis. In related magnetic alloys, microstructural features (internal boundaries) have been shown to trigger phase transformations with modified sharpness and reduced hysteresis, hinting at a critical role for grain size and interface density.
decision.unsolved: Despite composition-based tuning yielding large magnetocaloric effects, it remains unresolved whether and how controlled manipulation of the as-deposited microstructure can be used as an effective lever to broaden the first-order magnetostructural transition, thereby reducing the abruptness and hysteretic losses, while also enhancing the effective heat exchange. The boundaries over which these effects are operative (e.g., grain sizes below ~100 nm) and the trade-offs with mechanical stability have not been systematically explored.
decision.lever: Systematically tuning the deposition process parameters (such as substrate temperature and deposition rate) to achieve nanocrystalline grain refinement (targeting grain sizes below ~100 nm) in FeMnNiGeSi alloys
decision.why: This intervention directly tests the hypothesis that increased density of microstructural interfaces governs the kinetics and reversibility of the magnetostructural transition. By comparing the magnetocaloric response of as-deposited baseline samples with those processed to have refined grain sizes, one can observe whether the transition becomes broadened with lower peak entropy change and reduced hysteresis, as predicted. This approach follows the historical shift from single-variable, composition-only optimizations toward multi-variable process-controlled microstructure tuning, as indicated by prior work.
